summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated territory of the United States and stands under the United States national framework for identity documents, entry and visa policy; the findings below are those specific to the territory.

The territory does not license marriages between two people of the same sex read under birth-sex status, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot marry here. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 federal marriage ruling does apply and that the High Court of American Samoa would have to issue a certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; the litigation path runs to that court against the Territorial Registrar and then to the United States Department of the Interior. No same-sex couple has applied for a licence, so the question remains untested. Under the Respect for Marriage Act, the territory must recognise, though not perform, such marriages lawfully entered elsewhere, with equal treatment to opposite-sex couples, since 13 December 2022.

Local officials have proceeded on the premise that the ruling does not automatically apply. The Attorney General said in July 2015 that applicability was still under review, leaving American Samoa the only United States territory then unsure, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it; the Governor cited the preamble, the territorial constitution, Christian values and unincorporated status. In January 2016 the Fono Senate unanimously confirmed Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told legislators he had not read the federal ruling and that the district court "doesn't deal with this ruling", saying he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local law changed.

The territory deliberately declined a formal marriage ban in 2003: a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster to outlaw same-sex marriage was rejected by the Fono Senate on 20 March 2003 after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed. Fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified at the committee hearing that fa'afafine are men who express femininity through dress and speech and do not seek marriage with other men, citing Christian upbringing.

Consensual adult conduct is not criminalised. The 1963 sodomy statute made male homosexual and heterosexual sodomy illegal and did not address lesbian sex; the Fono revised the law in 1979 so that consensual sodomy ceased to be illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to consent through mental illness, effective 1980. The age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and "daughter".

Trans-specific violence and protection machinery is documented. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. A June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with the sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

The territory is widely described as tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities, with a long-standing practice of raising some boys as girls to take on a domestic role in communal life; fa'afafine, defined as born male and embodying male and female traits, are described as a recognised and integral part of traditional culture. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. American Samoan society is highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality predominate.
tangentialFactors:
Local expectations sit alongside a wider regional picture. Reserved behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, but homosexuality is described as widely accepted within Samoan culture, in contrast to the homophobia reported in Fiji, and the fa'afafine tradition is presented by local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin as making the Samoan islands "the homeland of fa'afafine culture". Western gay men are reported to be courted by fa'afafine locals and by men who present as straight.

American Samoa and the neighbouring country of Samoa share the fa'amatai chiefly system, and a university research guide frames the present period as a reclaiming of regional gender identities after a history of suppression.
localsOnly:
The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption. The Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted that ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals: it will change the name on a birth certificate on presentation of a name change order, and it may change the gender marker on production of medical documentation of the sex change.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, is the main community organisation, re-anchored to cultural pride, organising annual events and festivals and campaigning for the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions; beauty pageants within the fa'afafine community are popular, and families generally attend in numbers to support candidates.
outOfScopeNotes:
No same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence in the territory, so the question of whether the local practice survives challenge has no local test case. The constitutional durability of the local ban was the subject of an on-island survey reported in July 2024 by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether it would survive a challenge under the Fourteenth Amendment; as of mid-2024 the ban was treated on-island as operative and the question remains open. The 2026 law review article separates the law as written from the practical reality of local administration.

Sources record discrete incidents of violence and harassment rather than any rate, and no general homicide or violence figure for the territory is available in them, so no comparison between trans-specific and background violence can be made.
